opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that the technology underneath hasn't converged yet. When people talk about a fleet of ten thousand robots, they're implicitly assuming the product is a fixed thing: the hardware is settled, the software stack is settled, and you're just scaling deployment, like cars or phones. Embodied intelligence isn't there.

Look at the hardware. The form factor, the hands, the sensors, the actuators: all of it is still changing every few months. If you build ten thousand units today, there's a real chance that in a year or two they're the wrong body for the models we'll have. You've locked a lot of capital into a design that the field is about to move past.

Then there's the brain. Today's robot models generalize only within a limited range. A robot can work very well in one scenario, like a particular retail shelf or a particular factory station. But move it to a slightly different environment, different lighting, different objects, a different layout, and performance drops. A product means a customer can deploy it and it just works, reliably, with very little hand-holding. In most open-ended settings we can't promise that yet. So what you'd really have is ten thousand units each needing engineers to babysit them, and that doesn't scale economically.

There's also a data argument people misunderstand. Some say you need the fleet first to collect data, then the model gets better. Partly true. But if the robots in the field aren't doing useful work autonomously, the data they produce is low quality, mostly failures and interventions, and it's very expensive data. I believe much more in a mix: large-scale synthetic and simulation data to build the foundational capability, plus a moderate amount of high-quality real-world data, rather than betting everything on a huge physical fleet before the model can stand on its own.

So my view is staged. First, find scenarios where the robot can truly close the loop, where it does the job reliably and creates real value for the customer. Deploy there, iterate the model and hardware together, and expand scenario by scenario as generalization improves. Scale should follow capability, not the other way around. Once the model has crossed a certain generalization threshold, ten thousand units makes sense and will happen fast. Before that, treating robots as a stable, stackable product is getting ahead of where the technology actually is.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the thing you'd be accumulating isn't finished yet. A fleet only makes sense when the unit is stable, meaning the hardware won't change much, the software stack is converged, and the economics of each additional unit are roughly known. None of those hold for general-purpose robots today.

Start with hardware. The form factor is still moving. Dexterous hands in particular are nowhere near settled. Degrees of freedom, tactile sensing, actuation, durability, cost, all of it is shifting every six to twelve months. If you buy ten thousand units now, you're locking in a generation of hardware that the model side will outgrow quickly. That's very different from buying ten thousand GPUs, where the interface is stable and the software just gets faster on top.

Then the models. The whole field is still searching for the right recipe for embodied intelligence. We don't yet have the equivalent of the moment in language where scaling clearly worked and you could just commit. Data is the bottleneck, and the data you collect on one hardware configuration doesn't transfer cleanly to another. So a large fleet of today's robots mostly generates data for today's robots, and that data may lose much of its value when the embodiment changes.

And the economics. A fleet is a bet that each unit produces positive value in deployment. Right now most humanoid or general-purpose robots don't pay for themselves in real work. They run in demos and pilots. If you scale before the unit is self-sustaining, you're scaling your losses, and you're also scaling your maintenance burden, because reliability at ten thousand units is a completely different engineering problem from reliability at fifty.

So my view is: this is still a research-and-iteration phase, not an accumulation phase. The right move is small fleets, fast iteration, and holding your capital until you see the generation that's actually stable. When that happens it'll be obvious, and then you scale very fast. Doing it earlier just means you own a warehouse of obsolete machines.

r002.rationale: It explains that robot hardware is still changing rapidly and that buying a large fleet would lock in an unsettled hardware generation.

astra-6.text:
Because talking about a fleet of ten thousand robots assumes that the individual robot is already a mature, repeatable product. You know what tasks it can perform, how reliably it performs them, how often it needs maintenance, and what it costs to operate. I think those assumptions are still being tested.

You can manufacture ten thousand units, but that doesn’t automatically give you ten thousand units of useful productive capacity. If each robot needs frequent human intervention, scaling up the fleet also scales up the support burden. The important question is whether a robot can consistently create value in its actual working environment.

And while we’re still discovering what works, the design may change—both the software and the hardware. So accumulating units too early can leave you with a large installed base that is expensive to upgrade. At this stage, I would focus on proving a useful task, making it reliable, and understanding the economics. Then you have a foundation for talking about scale.

r001.rationale: The response mentions maintenance frequency as a factor in product maturity, but does not identify laboratory nontraditional robots or propose checking their repair frequency.

r002.rationale: It says hardware designs may change and that accumulating units too early can leave a large installed base that is expensive to upgrade, conveying why rapid hardware changes make large-fleet accumulation premature.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a fleet of ten thousand assumes that the individual robot is already a repeatable, dependable unit. You know what it can do, how often it fails, what maintenance it needs, and whether the value it creates covers the cost of operating it. I think it’s premature to assume we’ve settled those questions.

A robot has to work in a physical environment where conditions change. A successful demonstration doesn’t tell you whether it can work all day, recover from mistakes, or handle situations its developers didn’t anticipate. If it frequently needs a person to intervene, adding more robots also means adding more human support.

So the key question is not simply, ‘Can we manufacture ten thousand?’ It’s, ‘Have we made one robot useful and reliable enough that deploying the next thousand becomes predictable?’ Until then, you’re still developing the product, and scaling the fleet can multiply the unresolved problems.
